Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: People are not what they seem
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together' directly conflicts with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' For a severe mugging-related PTSD profile, markedly fragmented recall and very easy verbal access to the trauma narrative are hard to reconcile as describing the same current memory presentation.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: The Memory node is internally incoherent for a severe mugging/robbery PTSD presentation: 'I can talk about what happened very easily' suggests low avoidance and relatively integrated, verbally accessible trauma memory, whereas simultaneously endorsing very vivid detailed recall and body-based painful reliving implies a highly sensory, distressing, poorly integrated trauma memory. This combination is possible in milder cases, but here it is hard to reconcile clinically within the same Memory profile. The Negative Appraisals items are coherent for robbery trauma, but the Memory selections do not fit cleanly with that node pattern or with the strong Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory linkage in the formulation.

issues.item: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
issues.explanation: This item is more characteristic of ongoing threat/safety behavior than of a pure negative appraisal. In this profile, Threat is not endorsed and all Threat-related edges are inactive, while the active formulation is specifically centered on a Memory ↔ Negative Appraisals loop. The mistrust items fit robbery-related appraisals, but 'Constant Vigilance' introduces a prominent current-threat theme that is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

vignette:
Rajan arrived for his first appointment with a quiet, careful manner that seemed to take up as little space as possible. He was thirty-two years old, married, and worked as a housekeeper at a mid-sized hotel in the suburbs of Chicago. He spoke with his hands folded in his lap, occasionally pressing his palm flat against his ribs as if checking that something was still there. He had been referred by his primary care physician after several visits for chest pain and shortness of breath that turned out to have no physical cause. Rajan knew this, but he also knew that the pain was real.

The event that had reshaped his world happened eight months earlier, on a cold November evening. He had just finished his shift and was walking the six blocks from the hotel to the bus stop, a route he had taken hundreds of times. A man came up behind him near the entrance to a parking garage, shoved him hard against the brick wall, and demanded his wallet. Rajan handed it over. The man punched him twice in the ribs, once in the jaw, and then ran. Rajan lay on the ground for several minutes, not because he couldn't get up, but because he was certain that if he moved, the man would return. What stayed with him most was not the punch to his face, but the feeling of the brick scraping through his jacket against his ribs, and the sound of his own breath leaving him in a thin, high whine.

In the weeks that followed, Rajan tried to push the memory aside. He did not tell his wife the full story; he said he had been pushed, that was all. But the memory did not stay in the past. It came back to him at unpredictable moments, and when it did, he felt a sharp, localized pain in his ribs, exactly where he had been hit. He would press his hand there, sometimes for minutes, waiting for it to pass. The images were extraordinarily clear-the texture of the brick, the angle of the man's elbow, the fluorescent light flickering above the garage entrance-but if anyone asked him what had happened, he found himself unable to form the words. He knew what he had lived through, but the sentences would not come. His mouth would go dry, his throat would tighten, and he would shake his head.

Rajan began to change how he moved through his days. He stopped taking the bus. Instead, he asked his wife to drop him off at work and pick him up, telling her it was more convenient. He started arriving an hour early so he could enter the hotel through the employee entrance while it was still light, and he would wait in the break room until his shift began. At work, he avoided the side corridor that led to the laundry room because it was dimly lit and narrow, and the feeling of a wall on both sides made his chest tighten. He did not tell his supervisor about any of this. He simply became the employee who always seemed to need a different route.

His view of people shifted quietly but profoundly. Before the mugging, Rajan had considered himself a trusting person. He held doors for strangers, made small talk with guests, believed that most people were decent. Now, he found himself watching everyone. When a guest stepped too close to him in the hallway, he felt a surge of alertness. When a coworker he did not know well walked up behind him, he would turn sharply, his hand rising before he could stop it. He had come to believe that people were not what they seemed, that anyone could turn dangerous without warning. The world, he now felt certain, was a dangerous place, and he had simply been naive not to see it before.

His wife noticed that he had grown distant. He no longer wanted to go to the grocery store with her on weekends. He stopped visiting his brother's family because their apartment building had a parking garage. He spent more time in the bedroom, lying on his side, his hand pressed to his ribs. She asked him if something was wrong. He said he was just tired.

What finally brought Rajan to seek help was a moment at work two weeks ago. A guest had tapped him on the shoulder from behind to ask for extra towels. Rajan had spun around, his arm raised, his heart pounding so hard he thought he might vomit. The guest stepped back, startled. Rajan apologized, finished his task, and then locked himself in a supply closet for twenty minutes, shaking. He realized then that he could not keep living this way. He did not want to be afraid of a world he used to move through easily. He did not want to be a husband who could not explain why he flinched at every touch. But when he sat in the waiting room before his first session, he could not find the words to describe what had happened, and he wondered if he ever would.
